problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-4y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4,\,x>0.
$$
worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda +2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 2.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-2}={c}_{1}{x}^{2}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2{c}_{1}x-2\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}-(-{c}_{1}) \\ {c}_{1} & =1\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
